questions.q: Which command shows only commits whose message contains the word 'price'?
questions.explain: --grep searches commit messages. --author filters by who made the commit.

questions.q: Which command lists only the commits that changed cart.js?
questions.explain: git log -- <file> limits the history to commits that touched that file.

questions.q: Krish edits menu.txt and stages it. What do the two commands print?
questions.code:
$ git add menu.txt
$ git diff
$ git diff --staged
options: git diff prints nothing; git diff --staged shows the change
git diff shows the change; git diff --staged prints nothing
questions.explain: git diff compares the working directory with the staging area. After git add they match, so it's empty. --staged compares the staging area with the last commit.

options: The commit two before the one you are on
questions.explain: ~n goes n parents back. HEAD~1 is the previous commit, HEAD~2 the one before that.

questions.q: Krish is in the middle of unfinished work when an urgent bug must be fixed. What should he do first?
questions.explain: git stash parks the unfinished changes and gives him a clean working tree. After fixing the bug he runs git stash pop.

questions.q: What is the difference between git stash pop and git stash apply?
options: pop applies the stash and removes it from the list; apply keeps it in the list
pop deletes your changes; apply saves them
questions.explain: Both bring the changes back. pop also drops the stash; apply leaves it so you can apply it again.

questions.q: Which statements about tags are true? (Choose all that apply.)
options: A tag gives a permanent name to one commit, such as v1.0
Annotated tags (-a) store a message, the tagger and a date
Tags are pushed automatically with git push
git push origin --tags uploads all tags
questions.explain: Tags must be pushed explicitly: git push origin v1.0, or git push origin --tags.

questions.q: You edited menu.txt (not staged) and want to throw the edit away. Which command?
questions.explain: git restore <file> (classic form: git checkout -- <file>) replaces the file with the last committed version. Uncommitted edits are lost.

questions.q: Your last commit is NOT pushed. You want to undo the commit but keep its changes staged. Which command?
questions.explain: --soft moves the branch back and keeps the changes staged; --mixed keeps them unstaged; --hard deletes them.

questions.q: A bad commit is already on GitHub and your teammates have pulled it. How do you undo it safely?
options: git reset --hard HEAD~1 and git push --force
questions.explain: revert adds a new commit that does the opposite. History isn't rewritten, so teammates aren't affected.

questions.q: Which reset mode can permanently delete your changes?
questions.explain: --hard resets the branch, the staging area AND your files. Uncommitted work is lost.

questions.q: After git checkout HEAD~2, Git says you are in 'detached HEAD' state. How do you get back?
questions.explain: Detached HEAD means you are looking at a commit, not a branch. Switching back to a branch returns you to normal.
